evidence_quotes.quote: artículo de investigación donde se analiza las vías por las que acceden al servicio de agua potable de red quienes residen en asentamientos informales de la periferia de la Región Metropolitana de Buenos Aires, Argentina.

A partir de una etnografía y otras herramientas de investigación, se argumenta que: 1) acceden a redes de agua potable por vías alternativas que requieren necesariamente de la coparticipación de vecinos
entrevistas semiestructuradas a funcionarios públicos e informantes clave, análisis de documentos públicos y de estadística descriptiva, entre otros

los últimos datos sobre provisión de agua potable en asentamientos informales arrojan que solo un 12% de la población que reside en ellos accede al servicio por medio de conexiones formales (techo 2016).

country.comment: The study examines informal settlements in the Buenos Aires Conurbation (Conurbano Bonaerense) within the Metropolitan Region of Buenos Aires (RMBA), Argentina, with ethnographic fieldwork in the settlement pseudonymized as Santa María.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Resumen and Ideas destacadas; PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 4, Figure 1

effect_estimate.comment: Primary empirical analysis is qualitative; all numerical coverage figures reported in the paper are secondary descriptive statistics drawn from AySA and TECHO reports to contextualize the ethnographic and institutional findings.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Across two public utility regimes (OSN, 1983–1993; AySA, 2006–2015) and one private concession (AASA, 1993–2006), informal settlement residents in the Buenos Aires Conurbation were excluded from standard turn-key utility network expansion (which depended on formal land tenure, municipal cadastre legalization, and public-works channels) and instead accessed piped drinking water only through targeted co-production schemes (Pro-agua, MPG, Agua + Trabajo) and political/social intermediaries (Peronist punteros and piquetero work cooperatives) that shifted labor, negotiation, and technical burdens onto inadequately trained and under-equipped residents, slowing works and producing precarious connections marked by frequent outages, pipe ruptures, low pressure, and contamination. Secondary descriptive statistics cited show that while ~78% of the RMBA population had piped water in 2015, only 12% of informal settlement residents had formal connections (2016), and by late 2015 AySA's Agua + Trabajo program had completed only 99 modules (408 km of pipe serving an estimated 165,294 people, with 484 modules unfinished) versus over 3,300,000 inhabitants incorporated or near incorporation in formal neighborhoods.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 4–5, Introducción; PDF pp. 9–10, Prácticas y políticas focalizadas; PDF pp. 12–15, Desde el barrio i & ii and Conclusiones

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative study (design ceiling of 2 under CODEBOOK §9). Direct empirical observation via 2011–2015 ethnographic fieldwork in Santa María, semi-structured interviews with utility/regulatory officials, brokers, and cooperative workers, and project plans/sketches directly documents how targeted co-production programs, municipal-utility-cooperative contracting, cadastre non-legalization, and political brokerage operate on piped water expansion and service quality.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 5, Introducción; PDF pp. 6–15, Prácticas y políticas focalizadas and Desde el barrio i & ii

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines informal land tenure preventing individual billing and unlegalized municipal cadastre status mapping the settlement as river (ELIGIBILITY: tenure, planning, service_area); delegation of trenching, construction labor, and technical problem-solving to residents and cooperatives causing slowdowns and rework (BURDEN: delay); and targeted co-production programs (Pro-agua, MPG, Agua + Trabajo), discretionary municipal/electoral selection of neighborhoods and cooperatives, political brokerage by punteros and piquetero organizations, fragmented multi-agency governance (OSN/AASA/AySA, municipalities, ETOSS, ENHOSA, INAES, SGBATOS), and insufficient state/union training and technical supervision (DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION: discretion, accommodation, participation, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination, bureaucratic_assistance).

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes access to piped drinking water networks (water_access), low rate of formal utility connections versus informal/alternative extensions (formal_connection), service coverage disparities across formal neighborhoods and informal settlements (service_coverage), delays and unfinished modules in network extension (delay), and recurrent service interruptions, pipe breaks, low pressure, and contamination (service_continuity, service_reliability, service_quality). Sanitation is explicitly set aside in Footnote 1 (PDF p. 3).
